title: Reading the heading
hook: a track title tells you the song and the artist before you press play; so does the line above each hymn
tomorrow: a hymn has many lines. which one do you read first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, larivaar: the Granth with its words joined, and its spaced twin, padched. Two good cases, one shared line: word by word. Before the words, though, there's a line in smaller print.

A song comes up in a playlist and before you press play, the screen has already told you things: the title, the artist, maybe that it's live or acoustic. You know the voice and the feel before the first note. Open the Granth to almost any hymn and there's the same kind of line above it, in smaller print. It isn't a title. It's for the ear. It tells you how this hymn should sound, and whose voice you're about to hear.
screen: `THE TRACK TELLS YOU FIRST.` → `A LINE IN SMALLER PRINT.` → `HOW IT SOUNDS, WHOSE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Read the heading left to right and it gives up three things. First, the raga: the musical mode the hymn is set in, with its own mood. Asa, Sorath, Bilaval. Before you know what the hymn says, you know how it should feel. Second, Mahala and a number: whose voice this is. Every Guru signs as Nanak inside the hymns, so the heading does the naming. Mahala one is Guru Nanak; Mahala five is Guru Arjan. Third, sometimes, the word ghar and a number. And here's the honest part: scholars differ on exactly what ghar told the musicians, a beat, a scale, a style. The Granth gives the label and doesn't explain it. At the start of a new section, the heading may also carry Ik Onkar, Satgur prasad: the One, reached by the Guru's grace. So here's the thing worth telling someone tonight. The Granth tells you how a hymn should sound, and whose voice it is, before it gives you a single word. The words arrive already dressed in a mood.
screen: `FIRST, THE RAGA: HOW IT FEELS.` · `MAHALA AND A NUMBER: WHOSE VOICE.` · `GHAR: A LABEL SCHOLARS DEBATE.` · `SOUND BEFORE WORDS.` · then, large: `THE HEADING TELLS YOU.`

segments.voice: Find three headings, in a gutka, a printed copy or an app. For each one, say the raga's name out loud, and tap the Mahala number on your knee, one tap for Guru Nanak, five for Guru Arjan. Then rest your hands, breathe, and let the last raga's name sound once more in your head, like a note held after the music stops.
Reading the heading: the small line above each hymn, naming its raga, the Guru's voice by Mahala and number, and sometimes its ghar. The sixth word of the year.
For the road: the heading tells you how it sounds and whose voice it is, before the first word. Six of twenty, heard.

howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib each hymn sits under a heading naming its raga and its author by Mahala number, sometimes with a ghar; kirtan singers sing the hymn in the raga its heading names.
